scenarios.name: Game starts with 5 kamons each, centre 10, round 0
A round starts and deals; with everyone passing the round advances to 1 and nothing else changes (cards are random, only chance-free facts asserted)
Kobayakawa card is set after the deal; round completes with no fight and no showdown (K value is random, not asserted)
Hidden hands: with no showdown no card is revealed
SWAP is offered; seats that do not swap keep discarded 0 (the swapped card value is random)
Every seat is asked KEEP or SWAP
Talk step runs for everyone and the round completes
A seat with 0 kamons cannot fight: seats 2 and 3 fight, seat 1 stays out of the showdown
A lone fighter stakes 1 and gets it back: kamons stay 5
Exactly one fighter: kamon back, card not revealed, centre unchanged, no showdown winner
Showdown of two: non-fighters stay unrevealed with total 0 (fighters' cards are random)
Showdown of three resolves to one winner taking the centre bonus (who wins is random)
Showdown with centre at least 1: centre loses exactly 1
Showdown: non-fighters are untouched and the centre pays 1 (which fighter loses is random)
Game ends after round 10; most kamons wins
Game ends after round 10; tied for most share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer suggests 4, so it is kept. Below 3 a showdown is just a duel with no one to bluff off the table. Above 5 the 15-card deck cannot cover a hand and a reserve for every player plus K (6 players would need 13 of the 15 cards, leaving swaps and discards nearly fully informative), and one player's choice matters less.

spec_choices.what: Table talk kept as a simultaneous poll broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The source requires simultaneous messages. Talk earns its place because interests conflict: a player can claim a high card to scare others into passing, or a low card to bait fighters when K is large.

spec_choices.what: Reserve cards stored as a hidden table list in seat order
spec_choices.why: Nobody may see a reserve card, and a player attribute cannot be hidden from its owner, so the reserves live on the table with visibility none.

spec_choices.what: The tie-break is coded as the largest (total * 100 - card)
spec_choices.why: Totals are at most 30, so this ranks by total first and by the lower card second. Cards are distinct, so the result is unique.

A thoughtful player weighs K against their card (a low card plus a big K can win), reads public discards and messages, bluffs about strength, and saves kamons near 0, because staying out also keeps them alive.

simplifications.what: A tie for most kamons at the end is a shared win rather than a declared draw
simplifications.why: The engine ranks by one expression and players level at the top share the win, which is how it expresses the source's draw.

variation.original_summary: Kobayakawa is a 3-6 player bluffing and betting game. Each player holds one hidden card. In a draw phase they may improve their card or change the shared Kobayakawa card. Players then bet a kamon to fight. Among the fighters, the lowest card adds the Kobayakawa value, and the highest total takes the pot plus one kamon from the centre. Most kamons at the end wins.

review.evidence: Always PASS never gains. The other players start with 15 kamons between them (at 3 players), and every contested fight moves a kamon from the centre to them, so their average rises above 5 and someone passes the passer: always PASS loses. Always FIGHT loses its stake whenever it holds a middle card against two or more fighters, and it is easy to exploit. Ties go to the lower card, not to a seat, so no seat has an edge. The lowest-card bonus means neither high nor low cards are safe, so the choices change the outcome.

In the reviewed variation the fight poll was simultaneous and silent. Whether a card wins depends mostly on how many others fight: a middle card wins against one opponent but not two. Players could only guess the field size, so a large share of results came from guessing rather than reading opponents.

There is a lot to learn: using K and the public discards to estimate card ranges, reading KEEP/SWAP as a signal, and managing stakes over 10 rounds. A weak player still wins some fights through the lowest-card bonus.
Cards are hidden and the discards are partial public signals. The value of a card depends on the opponents' likely cards and on how many of them fight, so inference is required.
Totals, the winner, pot transfers and the final kamon counts are all arithmetic on tracked numbers.

It fits the limits: one shuffle per round, fixed 10 rounds, 15 steps. However, the original's sequential fight information was removed and nothing replaced it. The playable review failed it for having no talk in a 3-5 player game with opposed interests.

problems: The fight decision depends strongly on how many others fight, but the simultaneous silent poll gives no way to learn or influence that, so the poll is largely blind guessing.
The game has 3-5 players with directly opposed (zero-sum) interests, which is exactly where bluff talk adds reasoning, yet the design was silent on talk and failed the playable check.

changes.what: Add one simultaneous, non-binding public talk step after the discards are announced and before the fight poll. Every player writes one short message at the same moment, then all messages are shown.
changes.why: Players can now claim strength, threaten to fight, or bluff to deter others. Listeners must judge those claims against K, the discards and past behaviour, which replaces the sequential information of the original with something to reason about.
changes.fixes: The fight decision depends strongly on how many others fight, but the simultaneous silent poll gives no way to learn or influence that, so the poll is largely blind guessing.

changes.what: State explicitly that messages may be false and bind nobody, and that the fight poll stays simultaneous so no seat speaks or acts last.
changes.why: Bluffing stays costly to believe, and no fixed seat gains a positional edge.
changes.fixes: The game has 3-5 players with directly opposed (zero-sum) interests, which is exactly where bluff talk adds reasoning, yet the design was silent on talk and failed the playable check.

keeps: One hidden card per player and a public Kobayakawa value K
Lowest card among the fighters adds K, and the highest total wins
Kamon stakes, the winner takes the pot plus 1 from the centre
A draw phase that can replace the card, with the discard shown face up as a public signal
A lone fighter wins without revealing
Most kamons at the end wins

recommendation.reason: The previous variation worked except for the missing talk. Adding a simultaneous bluff-talk step fixes the playability failure and makes the fight choice a matter of reading opponents.

variation.name: Kobayakawa Duel Rounds with Table Talk
variation.summary: Each round, players hold one hidden card and may swap it, publicly bluff about their strength, then simultaneously bet to fight. The lowest card among the fighters gains K, and the highest total takes the pot plus a kamon from the centre. Most kamons after 10 rounds wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Each player starts with 5 kamons. The centre starts with 10 kamons. The game lasts exactly 10 rounds.

EACH ROUND:
1. Deal. Shuffle a fresh deck of 15 cards numbered 1 to 15. Deal each player one face-down hand card, which only that player sees. Deal each player one face-down reserve card, which nobody sees. Turn one more card face up: this is the Kobayakawa card, value K. Announce K.
2. Draw choice. All players choose KEEP or SWAP at the same moment. A SWAP player discards their hand card face up, takes their reserve card as their new hand card, and looks at it. Reserve cards of KEEP players are not used. Announce every discarded card and who discarded it.
3. Talk. Every player writes one short public message at the same moment, without seeing the others' messages. Then all messages are shown to everyone. Messages may say anything, including false claims about one's card or intentions. Nothing said is binding.
4. Fight choice. All players choose FIGHT or PASS at the same moment. A player with 0 kamons must PASS. Each FIGHT player puts 1 kamon into the pot.
5. Resolve.
   - No fighters: nothing happens.
   - Exactly one fighter: that player takes their own kamon back. Their card is not revealed, and the centre pays nothing.
   - Two or more fighters: all fighters reveal their cards. Each fighter's total equals their card, except that the fighter with the lowest card adds K to it. The fighter with the highest total wins. If totals tie, the tied fighter with the lower card wins. The winner takes the whole pot. If the centre has at least 1 kamon, the winner also takes 1 kamon from the centre. Losing fighters lose their stakes.
6. Announce all fighters, revealed cards, totals, the winner, and every player's kamon count.
7. After round 10 the game ends.
variation.objective: After round 10, the player with the most kamons wins. If two or more players tie for most, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Talk gives the fight poll something to reason about. The game is zero-sum on the pot, so players disagree about who should fight. Each player wants weak rivals to fight into their strong card and strong rivals to stay out. A player with a middle card benefits from claiming 'I have 14, stay out' to shrink the field. A player who simply follows that claim and passes with a card that would have won forfeits the pot and the centre kamon. A player who believes a fake 'I'm passing' and fights a middle card into three fighters loses the stake. Players must weigh claims against K, the public discards, KEEP/SWAP signals and each speaker's honesty in earlier rounds. There is no cooperative option, so endgame unraveling does not apply. Always PASS loses whenever any contested fight occurs, and always FIGHT loses stakes against attentive players.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFFS PER ROUND. With m fighters, the winner nets +m: the pot of m, minus their own stake, plus 1 from the centre. Each loser nets -1. A sole fighter nets 0 and a passer nets 0. So EV(fight) = p(m+1) - 1, and fighting pays exactly when the win chance p exceeds 1/(m+1). The centre holds 10 kamons and pays at most 1 per round for 10 rounds, so the subsidy never runs out early. Seats are equal: every choice is simultaneous and the turn-order tie-break is gone.

WINNING STRUCTURE. With L the lowest fighter card and H the highest, the lowest fighter wins if H <= L+K. Otherwise the highest wins. No middle card can ever win. With two fighters, the lower card wins if H-L <= K. A tie (L+K = H) goes to the lower card, which is consistent.

SAMPLE TABLE, K=5, one opponent drawn uniformly from the 13 other cards, break-even p = 1/3:
- Card 1: wins against b in {2,3,4,6}, so p = 4/13 = 0.31. PASS.
- Card 8: wins against b in {1,2,9,10,11,12,13}, so p = 7/13 = 0.54. FIGHT.
- Card 15: wins against b in {1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9}, so p = 8/13 = 0.62. FIGHT.
With K >= 14 the lowest fighter always wins, so card 1 cannot lose. With 3 or more fighters any middle card has p = 0. The best action therefore depends on K, your own card, the discards and how many others fight. No option is strictly better.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the WINNER RULE:
- Always PASS: stays at 5. Other players gain from every contested round, because centre payouts add to their total. It loses almost every game against fighters.
- Always FIGHT: has positive EV only against random play, about 1/m per contested round from the subsidy. Against selective players it fights middle and weak cards into their strong ones. Example: K=5, holding card 1 against a fighter, it loses 9 of 13. It loses regularly, so it does not win or draw almost always.
- Always KEEP and always SWAP: card value is non-monotone in K, so neither choice dominates. A blind swap is a gamble that sometimes helps and sometimes hurts.
- Highest bid: not applicable, since the stake is fixed at 1.

No policy never loses. Every player can realistically win. The labelled rules match the arithmetic.

playable.evidence:
WHAT WORKS:
- Cards: 5 players x 2 cards + K = 11 of 15, so the deck suffices.
- Rules coverage: the zero-fighter, one-fighter, multi-fighter, tie, empty-centre and zero-kamon cases are all covered.
- Finite and arithmetic: the game is a fixed 10 rounds and is decided by kamon counts the game keeps.
- Limits: the stated complexity is within every limit (steps 15/20, choices 2/4, attributes 12/20, hidden 2/3, draws 1/1, rounds 10/40). Finding the lowest and highest among a variable set of fighters needs calc steps, but fits.
- Restrictions: no board, judge or clock is needed. The draw is a single shuffle with remove/append operations.

THE FAILURE: TALK. This is a 3-5 player game, and the design is silent on talk. The original's Fight phase was sequential, so later players could condition on earlier fight or pass choices. Making the choice simultaneous removed that, and nothing replaced it. Whether to fight depends heavily on who else fights:
- a middle card wins with 2 fighters but never with 3;
- the break-even p falls from 1/3 to 1/4 to 1/5 as fighters are added.
Players have opposed interests, since the game is zero-sum on the pot. Bluffing 'I'm fighting with a high card' to deter others costs a believer real kamons, which is exactly where talk belongs. Without it, the fight poll beyond the KEEP/SWAP signal is largely guessing about each other. The repeated-cooperation check is not applicable, because there is no cooperative option.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT A GOOD PLAYER CAN USE:
- Inference: K, their own card, every announced discard (which narrows the distribution of opponents' cards), opponents' KEEP/SWAP choices (keeping signals a card the holder likes given K) and fight history across 10 rounds.
- Action: they act on this through fold thresholds. The sample table above shows these thresholds move p between 0 and 1 depending on K and card position.

AGAINST POOR PLAY: a sensible player folds middle cards and weak extremes. An always-fighter or random fighter feeds them stakes. Over 10 rounds the reasoning player is clearly favoured.

HOW MUCH IS CHANCE: the fresh deal each round gives high per-round variance. I estimate roughly 50-60% of a single game's result is chance, but the deal is re-randomised 10 times and selective folding overcomes it.

WHEN EVERYONE PLAYS WELL: results come down to card luck, as in poker. There is no single hidden type deciding the game, so this is acceptable variety rather than a luck-only outcome.

required_changes: Playable: add a simultaneous free-text talk step after the discards are announced and before the Fight choice. All players write a public message, all messages are shown, then the simultaneous FIGHT/PASS poll runs. State that talk is not binding. Alternatively, make the Fight choice sequential starting with the previous round's winner, with the start rotating if there is no winner, so later fighters see earlier choices as in the original. If sequential order is used, rotate the start every round to avoid a fixed seat edge. Update steps_per_round (+1 or +2) and keep it at or below 20.

balanced.evidence: Payoff of one contest: each fighter stakes 1 and the winner takes the pot plus 1 from the centre. In a 2-way fight the winner nets +2 and the loser -1, so fighting breaks even at a win chance of 1/3. A lone fighter gets the stake back and nets 0. The centre holds 10 and pays at most 1 per round over 10 rounds, so it never runs out. Cards are distinct, so totals tie only when lowest+K equals another card, and then the lowest card wins. Win chance of hand c against one random opponent card (13 possible), worked out by hand. K=8: c=1 7/13 (54%), c=5 7/13, c=10 6/13, c=12 6/13, c=15 6/13. K=2: c=15 11/13 (85%), c=8 6/13, c=1 1/13. K=14: c=1 13/13 (unbeatable). No card or option is best for every K, so the fight decision depends on K, the discards and opponents' likely holdings. WINNER RULE for thoughtless policies. (a) Always PASS ends on exactly 5. Total kamons = 5n + C, where C is the number of contested rounds, so the other players average more than 5 whenever C>=1 and at least one of them has more than 5. Always-pass therefore loses in every game with any contest against sensible or random play. It only draws if nobody ever contests. It does not win or draw almost always. (b) Always FIGHT: if no one else fights it nets 0. When a sensible player joins, that player has chosen a card with more than 1/3 win chance against a random card, so always-fight loses more than its fair share at -1 each time. Against random play it is a coin-flip lottery. It loses to sensible play over 10 rounds and does not dominate. (c) Always SWAP or always KEEP: swapping replaces a known card with a uniformly random one. Keeping a strong card (for example 1 when K=14, or 15 when K=2) is clearly better, so neither pure policy dominates. Seats: every choice is simultaneous, and ties are broken by card value, not seat, so no seat has an edge. Any player can win. A tie for most kamons is a draw, which is symmetric. There is no labelled payoff ordering to check, and this is not a cooperation game, so the cooperation and late-defection test does not apply. In the last round a leader may pass to protect a lead, and the trailers must fight. That is legitimate endgame planning, not a dominant option.

playable.evidence: Cards needed per round: with 5 players, 5 hands + 5 reserves + K = 11, within 15, so the fresh-deck deal always works. Every situation is covered: no fighters, a lone fighter, 2+ fighters, ties, a player at 0 (must PASS but still swaps and talks), an empty centre (impossible by count, but handled anyway), and a tie for most kamons (draw). The game is finite at 10 rounds. The winner is decided by comparing kamon counts the game keeps. Complexity: steps 18 <= 20; choice steps 3 (swap, talk, fight) <= 4; attributes 13 <= 20; hidden elements 2 (hand card, reserve card) <= 3; 1 random deal per round <= 1; rounds 10 <= 40. Engine features: hidden_hands, simultaneous_choice, free_text_talk and fixed_rounds are supported. Comparing totals is arithmetic with `when`/`if`. Taking cards from the shuffled list uses the deck workaround. No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed. Talk is justified because interests conflict. A strong holder wants rivals to fight, since a lone fighter gains nothing. A weak holder wants to deter fights. Following another player's claim can cost a kamon. Claims can be checked against K, the public discards and the KEEP/SWAP choices. Talk is simultaneous, as the platform prefers.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance is substantial. The deal decides card strength each round, and I estimate about 50-60% of a single round's outcome is chance. Over 10 rounds, decisions accumulate. There is real material to infer from: K is public, every discard and who made it is announced, and a KEEP choice signals a card worth keeping. The swap itself is a risk decision, since the reserve is uniform over unseen cards. The fight decision has a clear threshold, a win chance above 1/3 against the likely fighting range, and that threshold shifts strongly with K (see the tables above). Talk adds bluffing and the reading of bluffs. A threshold player beats always-fight and random players in expectation by roughly 0.3-0.5 kamons per contested round, which is decisive when final counts differ by a few kamons. Under symmetric good play the deals break the tie. However, the deal is reshuffled every round and the outcome is the sum of 10 rounds of decisions, so good play overcomes a bad deal rather than chance alone deciding. Endgame planning also matters: leaders pass and trailers must fight.

triage.reason: The game applied the rule correctly. Seat 2 had 1 kamon after seat 1 fought HIGH (stake 2), so the game recorded PASS for it without asking: fight_choice = PASS, stake 0, kamons still 1, held_rounds now 1, and seat 1 took the pot as the sole fighter. The test failed only because it required a menu offering PASS. A forced pass with no menu has the same result under the rules.
triage.guidance: For the forced-pass scenario (and any rule that says a player 'must PASS'), do not require that a PASS option was offered. A game may skip the poll and apply the PASS automatically. Assert on the results instead: the constrained seat ends with fight_choice 'PASS', pays no stake (kamons unchanged at 1), and keeps its card (held_rounds becomes 1). Seat 1, the sole fighter, takes the pot (kamons 4 - 2 + 3 = 5) and pot returns to 0. It is fine to assert that the seat was never offered LOW or HIGH, but not that it was offered PASS.

triage.reason: The game was built and behaves as specified, but the design needs 22 steps per round, over the engine's limit of 20. The excess comes from the rules, not a coding mistake. A thoughtless 'always last option' policy also wins about half its games from seat 1, which hints that blind aggression pays too well.
triage.guidance:
Cut the per-round procedure by at least 3-4 steps while keeping the core bluff-and-fight loop. Candidates:
(1) Drop the SHIFT option and the Alternate card. The Kobayakawa is dealt once per round and never replaced, which removes the shift check, the alternate deal and its announcement.
(2) Merge the two-stage draw: replace KEEP/DRAW followed by the OLD/NEW choice with one simultaneous choice, KEEP or SWAP. SWAP takes the reserve card blind and discards the old card face up. This removes the separate private look and the second poll.
(3) Remove the round-10 special cases: use the same minimum stake and centre feed every round, and always carry a tied pot (split ties only at game end, or simply let a final tie remain in the pot).
(4) Optionally drop the simultaneous TALK step, or fold the reveal announcements into the fight prompt.
Also blunt reckless fighting so that always choosing the last option (HIGH) is not a near-50% strategy. For example, when two or more players fight, a losing HIGH fighter could lose one extra kamon to the centre. Or the Kobayakawa bonus could go only to the lowest card when that fighter fought LOW.

triage.reason: The rule only says a player with 0 kamons must PASS. The game does this by setting seat 1's fight choice to PASS automatically instead of polling a one-option menu, and seat 1 never fought or staked. The test fails because it insists the forced PASS be shown as an offered option, which is a detail of how the move is presented, not of the rules' outcome.
triage.guidance: Rewrite the 'A seat with 0 kamons can only PASS' scenario so it checks results, not whether a 'PASS' option was offered. Give seat 1 0 kamons and have the other seats fight. Then assert that seat 1 is not among the fighters: its revealed_card and total stay 0, its kamons stay 0, and winner_seat is never 1. Also assert that the pot and showdown resolve using only the other fighters. Accept either way of handling the 0-kamon player: a poll offering only PASS, or an automatic PASS with no poll. Do not assert on options_include for a player whose choice is forced.
